field_decisions.value: Distinct proposed versions: House H.5175 proposes chapter 164 section 163, defining a data center by a designed load of at least 20 MW and digital-data purpose. Specified new or expanded data centers seeking permits from the department or the energy facilities siting board would procure sufficient electricity for operational needs using at least 80% renewable resources; those seeking a Department of Environmental Protection permit to operate fossil-fuel backup generation would first demonstrate on-site battery storage infeasibility. The House also proposes data-center tariffs protecting other ratepayers and incentivizing efficiency. Senate S.3166 section 3 proposes conditions for specified data-center tax benefits; sections 88 and 114 propose flexible interconnection and a working group including data-center representatives. The excerpts do not establish enactment of either version or the provisions' present force.

facts.value: Massachusetts 194th General Court H.5175, titled An Act relative to energy affordability, clean power and economic competitiveness, is the House-adopted, amended text of H.5151.
The retained excerpts identify the House text and Senate reprint but do not name a sponsor. Reprint attribution does not establish sponsorship.
The Senate amended H.5175 by replacing everything after the enacting clause with S.3143 text; S.3166 is the Senate text reprinted as amended. The House and Senate provisions are distinct texts.

House section 54 proposes chapter 164 section 163. It defines a data center as a facility designed for at least 20 MW whose primary purpose is digital-data storage, management and processing, including specified related infrastructure.

A new or expanded data center seeking a permit from the department or the energy facilities siting board would have to procure sufficient electricity for operational needs using at least 80% renewable energy resources.

A new or expanded data center seeking a Department of Environmental Protection permit to operate fossil-fuel backup generation would first have to demonstrate that on-site battery energy storage is infeasible.

Each electric company would file for a data-center electricity tariff designed to protect other ratepayers from increased costs caused by data-center demand and incentivize efficiency, including use of captured heat. The department would review and approve compliant applications.

House section 68E would require each electric company to file its tariff application within 180 days after the act's effective date and apply the tariff to each data center in its service area within one year.

Senate section 3 proposes conditions for receiving, maintaining or renewing specified sales-tax benefits, covering clean energy, efficiency and grid impacts, water, environmental and health effects, labor, community benefits, economic development and accountability. The executive office could condition, suspend, revoke, limit or decline an exemption for noncompliance; other applicable requirements would remain in place.

Senate section 88 proposes chapter 164 section 157, requiring distribution companies to offer department-approved flexible interconnection programs for new customer loads and distributed energy resources, based on curtailment arrangements. This is a general interconnection provision, not the House's data-center-specific tariff.

Senate section 114 proposes a sustainable economic development zones working group, including data-center representatives, to address connection delays and recommend infrastructure, tariff and financing options. It would convene within 60 days and report within 10 months after the effective date; DPU action and an update would follow on stated deadlines.
On February 26, 2026, the House passed H.5175 to be engrossed, 128 yeas to 27 nays, Yea and Nay No. 141. On February 27, H.5151 was published as amended.

On March 2, 2026, the Senate read and referred the bill to Senate Ways and Means. On June 23 it adopted an order relative to subject matter. On June 25 it listed additional Senate bills as bases, recommended replacing the text and title, and placed the bill in the orders for July 1.

On July 1, 2026, the Senate read the bill a second time, substituted S.3143 text, reprinted it as S.3166, ordered and gave it a third reading, and passed it to be engrossed, 32 yeas to 8 nays, Roll Call 205.

The latest displayed actions are July 16, 2026: both branches suspended rules; the House non-concurred and appointed Cusack, Michlewitz and Jones to conference; the Senate insisted on its amendment and appointed Barrett, Creem and Tarr in concurrence. The excerpts do not establish enactment.
